title: The bell of the customs house
bodyMd:
Historians who study the spread of clock time often tell it as a story of employers imposing discipline on reluctant workers. The records of Montalbero, a cloth-making town in the northern Apennines, tell a more tangled story.

In 1437 the town council voted to buy a bell for the tower of the customs house and to have it rung at dawn, at midday and at dusk. The minutes record that the request came not from the wool merchants, as one might expect, but from the fullers' guild. Its members worked in shifts at the river and needed to know when the right to use the water passed from one workshop to the next. The merchants opposed the expense, and the bell was bought only after the fullers agreed to pay half of its cost from their own funds.

Complaints came instead from the weavers, who worked at home and had no need to coordinate with anyone. Their petition of 1441 does not object to the hours the bell announced, which were the hours they already kept. It objects that the bell was in the council's keeping, so that "the day of the town" now belonged to whoever held the rope. The weavers asked for a second bell to be hung in the guild's own chapel. The council refused.

It would be easy to read all this as a victory for control from above. But the fines ledger points the other way. In the twenty years after the bell was installed, the council recorded only eleven fines for arriving late to work, against several hundred for selling short measures of cloth. Whatever the bell did, it seems not to have been used as a whip.

The lesson is not that the bell was harmless. It is that a single object served different groups in different ways: a timetable for the fullers, a grievance for the weavers and, for the council, a small but visible sign of who spoke for the town. An account that gives it only one meaning has read only one set of records.
